clue.text: Country depicted in jacket of Rabelais book

indicators.note: the country is pictured inside the jacket letters, so it goes between them
a jacket is the outer layer, so only the first and last letters of Rabelais are kept

parts.note: the word whose outside letters are taken
Oman is a country on the Arabian peninsula

explanation.surface: A country is illustrated on the dust jacket of a Rabelais volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jacket of' gives RS, the outside of Rabelais, and OMAN is 'depicted in' it. Romans is a book of the New Testament, Paul's letter to the church in Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Romans is the Epistle to the Romans, one of the books of the Bible.

clue.text: Writer gulps high tea if blissful

indicators.note: the pen swallows the other letters, so they go inside it

parts.note: a Bic is a ballpoint pen, a writer

indicators.note: high as in intoxicated, so the letters of tea are scrambled

parts.note: the word whose letters are rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer greedily swallows a high tea, if happy enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high' scrambles TEA into EAT, and with IF that is what BIC, the pen, 'gulps'. High tea is a British early-evening meal, which is why 'high' slips past as part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatific describes a look of serene, saintly joy, so it is close to blissful.

clue.text: Now and then, pair stay in city of 1

indicators.note: Something that happens now and then happens at intervals, so letters are taken at intervals — every other one.

parts.note: take the first, third, fifth and seventh of these eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a couple pausing somewhere in Italy, and the instruction hides in the ordinary phrase that opens the clue. Cross-references like 'of 1' point at another entry's answer, not its number.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross-reference makes this 'a city of the Romans': the Tuscan town was a Roman colony, so the definition names it by its ancient rulers.

clue.text: Pastime of six, thoroughly discontented after start of play

indicators.note: A word robbed of its contents keeps only its shell, so everything between the first and last letter of 'thoroughly' goes.

parts.note: a script labels its opening Act I, with the Roman numeral one
six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: It fixes the running order: the two short chunks follow the opening of the play rather than coming before it.

parts.note: the outer letters of that ten-letter adverb

explanation.walkthrough: Two Roman numerals arrive by different routes — one dressed up as the first scene of a play, one as the plain number. 'Of six' reads as part of the pastime, which is where the join hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastime is a leisure pursuit, and the answer is the broader noun for anything you occupy yourself with — a general word standing in for a narrower one.

clue.text: Tragic heroine's flogged in Irish domain

indicators.note: Here it is not a preposition of place but the instruction to bury one word inside another.

parts.note: .ie is Ireland's internet country domain; this is its first letter
to flog something is to sell it, and the past tense is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Web addresses ending .ie are Irish, and setters use national domains as ready-made two-letter chunks. 'Tragic' is doing definition work here rather than decorating the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish princess of the Tristan legend, who dies of grief at the end of Wagner's opera, is a textbook example of a tragic heroine.

clue.text: Say Dorothy's served up heavy food

indicators.note: Food is served up at table, but in a down entry 'up' also tells you the letters climb back the way they came.

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for 'say' in the sense of for example
Dot is the pet form of Dorothy, and the possessive S rides along

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as dinner being brought out, and every word of it turns out to be an instruction. Dot for Dorothy is a nickname setters rely on constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means filling, starchy stuff — suet pudding, dumplings — so 'heavy food' is a plain synonym for it rather than a description.

clue.text: Passes NY's bustling electrified junctions

indicators.note: A bustling street is full of people pushing past each other, so the letters will not keep their places.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder; the possessive S belongs to the surface only

explanation.walkthrough: 'Passes NY' looks like commuter geography rather than raw material, and 'bustling' is exactly the word a New York surface wants — which is why it does not read as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the junctions between nerve cells, where an electrical impulse jumps a tiny gap, so the definition describes the things literally.

clue.text: I put the end of Endymion in the middle of poem

indicators.note: the setter tells us to place one piece somewhere, here in the middle letters
the end letter goes inside the pair taken from poem
the middle letters of poem, dropping its first and last

parts.note: the word whose central letters are taken

indicators.note: only the last letter of Endymion is used

parts.note: Keats's long poem, here only supplying its last letter

explanation.surface: A poet sets the closing part of Endymion, Keats's poem, at the centre of a new work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the end of' Endymion is N; 'the middle of' poem is OE; N is 'put in' between them. 'I' is the Roman numeral for one.
explanation.definitionFit: I is the Roman numeral for the number one, as well as a pronoun meaning oneself.

clue.text: Constantly breaking Nancy's tiles

indicators.note: Something broken comes apart into pieces you then put back together differently, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder, apostrophe ignored as usual

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a clumsy guest wrecking a bathroom. The definition is the very first word, which is the place solvers tend to look last in a long anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs meaning without ever stopping; the answer insists on the absence of any break, where the definition stresses steadiness.

clue.text: Dead wrong about thin gravy — temperature is changed

indicators.note: Letters in the wrong order are not in the order the clue prints them, so they have to be put right by rearranging.
To write about a subject is to go round it, and here the shuffled letters go round the gravy.

parts.note: four letters of fodder
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature
jus is the thin pan juice a chef serves in place of thick gravy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead wrong' is one phrase on the surface and two separate instructions underneath, and the dash conceals where the fodder stops. Jus is worth learning as a three-letter gravy.
explanation.definitionFit: To adjust something is to change it by a small deliberate amount, so 'changed' is the past-tense synonym with the fine-tuning left implicit.

clue.text: Do you briefly join a western den of insurance workers?

parts.note: to do a part is to act it
U is the short texting form of you

indicators.note: in an across clue a western route runs right to left, so den is read backwards

parts.note: a lair is an animal's den

explanation.surface: An invitation to join a gang of insurance clerks in their lair out West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is the verb act, as in doing a part; 'western' means read right to left, the way one travels west on a map, so the den runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Actuaries are the statisticians who calculate insurance risks, and actuarial is the adjective for their work.

clue.text: Law set by head of administration in province of 1D

parts.note: the actor Jude Law: the surname is printed and the first name is wanted

indicators.note: The head of a word is its leading letter, so only the front of 'administration' is taken.

parts.note: its opening letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Law' wants to be statute in a clue full of administration; it is a surname instead, and the cross-reference at the end makes the definition a Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: Under Rome the southern part of what is now Israel and the West Bank was administered as its own province, the one Pilate governed.

clue.text: Protected documents a felon guards

indicators.note: To guard something is to keep it under cover, which is what these two clue words are doing to a run of letters.

parts.note: four consecutive letters straddle the gap between the first two of these

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words hide best inside a phrase that sounds like a complete thought, and 'documents a felon guards' is one, so nothing draws the eye to the join.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Protected' swaps in as an adjective — out of harm's way — while the surface pushes the noun sense, the strongbox that documents are kept in.

clue.text: Endlessly varied loons in America

indicators.note: A word taken endlessly loses the letter on its end, so the adjective arrives one short.

parts.note: varied in the sense of assorted or sundry

explanation.walkthrough: The birds are the whole point: what North America calls loons, Britain calls divers, so the definition is doing geography as well as ornithology.
explanation.definitionFit: The big fish-eating waterbirds Americans know as loons are called by the answer's name in Britain — same birds, two national vocabularies.

clue.text: Right to leave archer for divine Greek lady

indicators.note: What leaves is taken out: the abbreviation named just before it walks out of the word that follows.

parts.note: the bow-carrying god of love, who shoots his arrows at people
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.walkthrough: Archery points at Cupid under his Greek name, and losing one letter of him leaves the rosy-fingered goddess of the dawn — a neat piece of mythological sleight of hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A divine Greek lady is a goddess, and this is the dawn goddess of Greek myth, so the definition names her by category.

clue.text: Volcano's sulphur removed from bubbling toxic soap

indicators.note: the sulphur letter is taken out of the fodder before it is rearranged
a bubbling mixture is stirred up, so the remaining letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: A volcano's sulphur has been taken out of a fizzing poisonous soap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removed from' takes the S out of TOXIC SOAP, leaving TOXICOAP, and 'bubbling' rearranges those eight letters. Cotopaxi is an active volcano in the Andes of Ecuador.
explanation.definitionFit: Cotopaxi is one of the highest active volcanoes in the world, in Ecuador.

clue.text: Wings quit fancy show with covers from Vanity and Fish

indicators.note: the wings are the outside letters, so each of fancy and show loses its first and last

parts.note: the first word to lose its wings, its outside letters
the same wing-clipping instruction applies to show as well, which loses S and W to leave its inner pair

indicators.note: covers are the outside, so the first and last letters of Vanity

parts.note: the word whose outer letters are taken

explanation.surface: Someone flew off from a fancy show with covers of Vanity Fair, the magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings quit' clips both fancy and show, giving ANC and HO; 'covers from' Vanity gives VY. The surface leans on Vanity Fair, the magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: The anchovy is a small, strongly flavoured sea fish, often salted or tinned.

clue.text: Australian politician greeting school's crustacean

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for Australian
an MP is a Member of Parliament
the everyday two-letter hello
whales travel in a school, also called a pod

explanation.walkthrough: Four short pieces laid end to end and nothing moved, which is what keeps a long charade fair. School and pod are interchangeable for whales, not for fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandhoppers and freshwater shrimps belong to this order of small many-legged crustaceans, so the definition names the wider group they sit in.

clue.text: They print letters on electoral system

indicators.note: In an across entry 'on' puts the thing before it after the thing after it, so the letters follow the system.

parts.note: PR is proportional representation, the voting system Britain keeps arguing about
written out in full the letter S is an ess, and more than one of them are esses

explanation.walkthrough: Spelling a letter out as a word — ess for S, em for M, ex for X — is a device worth owning, and here the plural of one does all the heavy lifting.
explanation.definitionFit: 'They print' defines by function rather than by synonym: these are the machines that put ink on paper, and by extension the newspaper trade itself.

clue.text: Corporation's year under pressure from drug ring

indicators.note: in a down entry the year letter sits underneath, pressed down by the drug and ring above it

parts.note: pot is slang for cannabis
to ring is to bell, as in sounding a bell

explanation.surface: A company's year is spent under pressure from a drugs ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is an old jocular word for a large belly, not a company. Y goes 'under' POT and BELL in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is old slang for a paunch, so it means a potbelly, the large rounded stomach.

clue.text: Notice habitual junkie Holmes is finally clean

parts.note: to spot something is to notice it

indicators.note: It asks for the closing letter of each of the four clue words in front of it, taken in order.

parts.note: the last letters of those four, read left to right

explanation.walkthrough: Sherlock really was a habitual cocaine user, so the surface is fair as well as funny — and the clue still only wants the final letter of his name. Four words clipped in a row is a lot of concealed work.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Clean' and the answer are both adjectives for having no mark on you, literally or by reputation, which is why either can end this sentence.

clue.text: Essentially happy community cabin?

indicators.note: The essence of a word is at its heart, so each of the three that follow gives up only its central letter.

parts.note: the middle letter of five
the central letter of nine
the middle letter of five again

explanation.walkthrough: Read once, the clue is a fair description of the thing itself; read again, the same words are three middle letters. The question mark is the setter flagging that double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition: a village local really is the cheerful shared room a community treats as its own front room.

clue.text: Corpses' nasty smell fades away

parts.note: BO is the familiar shorthand for the smell of stale sweat
a sound or a light that fades away dies

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a whiff in a changing room and the definition is a mortuary, which is a long way to travel in six letters. BO for body odour is an initialism setters take as read.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpses are the dead, and the answer is the plain plural noun a police report uses for them — the same word that means the living kind.

clue.text: How Eastender says "fingers crossed he consumed drug"

indicators.note: an East End Londoner, a Cockney, drops the H sounds when speaking

parts.note: crossing fingers is hoping, so this is 'hope he ate'

explanation.surface: A Cockney hopes some lad has taken his drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney drops the H, so 'hope he ate' comes out as 'ope 'e ate, which runs together as the answer. An Eastender is someone from London's East End, home of Cockney speech.
explanation.definitionFit: An opiate is a narcotic drug derived from opium, such as morphine.

clue.text: Block Mev's editor interrupting exercises

parts.note: Mev is the setter, so 'Mev's' is I'm, Mev is

indicators.note: the editor letters break into the middle of the exercises abbreviation

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises

explanation.surface: An editor breaks into the setter's gym session to block his work.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter names himself, so 'Mev's' gives I'M; ED is 'interrupting' PE.
explanation.definitionFit: To impede is to obstruct or hinder, which is what blocking something does.

clue.text: Promise the return of some imprisoned rowdies

indicators.note: Something returning comes back the way it went, so the buried letters are read from right to left in this across entry.
'Some' means a part and not the whole, the standard signal that only a run of letters inside the phrase is wanted.

parts.note: four consecutive letters straddle the gap between these two, and they are picked up backwards

explanation.walkthrough: 'Imprisoned' is surface rather than instruction, which is what makes this hard — the concealment is signalled by the innocuous 'some', and the whole thing reads as a court report.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving your promise is giving your word: the noun sense of a personal undertaking, as in 'word of honour'.

clue.text: European article following old comedian's simple task

indicators.note: What follows comes afterwards, so the article is placed below the comedian in this down entry.

parts.note: Ken Dodd, the tickling-stick comic from Liverpool, a British household name for fifty years
the French for 'the'

explanation.walkthrough: 'European article' is the setter's standard way of asking for a foreign 'the', with French and German both fair game — the crossing letters settle which one is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is British informal for something that takes no effort at all, so 'simple task' matches it noun for noun.

clue.text: Asian god's atrocious nadir

indicators.note: Something atrocious is badly done, and badly arranged is what happens to the letters beside it.

parts.note: five letters of fodder, the word for a lowest point

explanation.walkthrough: 'Atrocious nadir' sounds like one gloomy phrase, which is how the instruction manages to stand right beside its own fodder without being noticed.
explanation.definitionFit: The thunder-wielding king of the gods in the Vedas, so 'Asian god' defines by example, picking one name out of the Hindu pantheon.

clue.text: Quiet clergyman was sick, came through

parts.note: p is piano, the musical direction to play softly
Rev. is the abbreviation for a Reverend
to ail is to be unwell

explanation.walkthrough: Two abbreviations and then a plain synonym, with the comma the only sign of where the definition starts. P for piano is worth keeping: it is how music writes 'quiet'.
explanation.definitionFit: To come through an ordeal is to survive it and end up on top, which is the past-tense verb the answer supplies.

clue.text: Small number of sports administrators raised two points

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something turns it upwards, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: the FA, the Football Association, runs English football
E and W, east and west, are two compass points

explanation.surface: A few sports officials put two points to a vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns FA upwards to AF; E and W are compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: A few means a small number of things or people, the idiomatic phrase for several.

clue.text: Go live under crooked gorge

indicators.note: Crooked means bent out of true, and letters bent out of true no longer sit in the order printed.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder — the whole of the clue except its last two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go live' is broadcasting jargon and 'under' looks like a positional instruction, so the fodder does not read as fodder at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To gorge is to eat far more than you should, which is the verb the answer supplies in a slightly politer register.

clue.text: Very large source of light for 1D

parts.note: so = very, as in 'so tired'
L is the clothing-label abbreviation for large

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is the whole trick: 1 down supplies the language, so the light source has to be named in Latin rather than English.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin's word for the sun — and 1D names the people whose language that was, so the definition asks for the daylight source under its Roman name.
